title: Q2: which gods hold the body? breath proves itself by leaving (2)
hook: the powers of the body brag that they hold it up, and breath settles the argument by starting to walk out
tomorrow: Q3: where does breath come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first question, rayi and prana, and your line, the two paths of the sun. Matter and breath, the moon and the sun. Did your good works and your inner work each get a few minutes? Day four hundred seven.

A group project, the night before it's due. Who really carried this? The one who wrote it says the writing. The one who presented says the presentation. The one who booked the room says nobody would've had anywhere to meet. Then the quiet one who did the actual research gets up to leave, and suddenly everyone realizes what they were standing on. Bhargava, from Vidarbha, the second student, asks Pippalada: how many gods hold up a living being? Which of them make it shine? And which one is the greatest? Pippalada answers with exactly that argument.
screen: `WHO REALLY CARRIED THIS?` → `THE QUIET ONE GETS UP TO LEAVE.` → `WHICH GOD IS GREATEST?`

segments.voice: The gods of the body, Pippalada says, are space, wind, fire, water and earth, and speech, mind, the eye and the ear. One day they shine with pride and declare: we hold up this body. We keep it standing. Then breath, prana, the chief of them all, says: don't be deluded. It's me. I divide myself five ways, and I hold it up. They don't believe him. So breath, out of pride, begins to rise, as if to leave. And as he rises, all the others are pulled up with him. When he settles back down, they all settle. The text gives a picture any village would know. When the king bee rises, all the bees rise. When it settles, they all settle. So it was with speech, mind, eye and ear. Then the gods, convinced, sing breath's praises. He burns as fire. He is the sun, the rain, the wind, the earth. He is what is and what isn't, and what never dies. Near the start of this year, in the Chandogya, the powers of the body had the same quarrel, and each one took a turn leaving. Here the story is quicker and sharper. Breath doesn't wait for the others to try. He just begins to stand, and that's enough. Notice what the story is saying about the body. Speech, sight and mind are real powers. But they all ride on something none of them can do without. In the story, nobody notices breath until it starts to go.
screen: `SPEECH, MIND, EYE, EAR: WE HOLD IT UP.` · `BREATH: IT'S ME, DIVIDED FIVE WAYS.` · `BREATH RISES; ALL RISE WITH IT.` · `LIKE BEES WITH THEIR KING.` · then, large: `PRANA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one who holds the house up. Sit, and breathe normally. Then, gently, at the top of an in-breath, pause, just for a moment, nothing strained. See whether everything seems to wait: the thoughts, the listening, even the sense of the room. Then let the breath go on, and feel it all start moving again. Do that two or three times, softly, and then just let breath carry the body without your help. The bell holds the time.
Prana, breath, the chief of the body's powers. Speech, mind, eye and ear all claim to hold the body, until prana begins to leave and they all rise with it.
Your line: when breath left, all left. Today, notice the quiet person or thing everything else depends on, and thank it before it has to get up and leave. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Breath (prana) is honored in many Hindu practices, from pranayama in yoga to the five pranas offered with the first mouthfuls of a meal in some traditional households.

original.note: Sanskrit prāṇa, breath, life: the chief of the body's powers in Prashna 2.

trapdoor: what you thought: the brain runs the body; breath is just background.
what it means: in the Prashna, speech, mind and senses all ride on breath, which proves it by starting to leave.
what a scholar hears: madhukararāja, the king bee (Prashna 2.4): when it rises, the whole swarm rises with it.
